headline: Germany: cannabis pharmacies propose adult-use sales pilot
dek: Germany's VCA pharmacy group proposes a supervised pilot selling cannabis without prescription; France pushes its medical decree to January 2027.
key_points: The Association of Cannabis-Dispensing Pharmacies (VCA) proposed on 23 November a supervised pilot letting pharmacies sell cannabis to registered adults without a prescription.
Drug Commissioner Hendrik Streeck questioned leaving Germany's roughly five million users to dealers, but his office says he has not endorsed pharmacy sales.
In France, Health Minister Stéphanie Rist told the National Assembly on 24 November that the HAS evaluation decree goes to the Council of State in January 2027.
Only about 400 French patients remain on treatment from the 2021 pilot, down from 700 in early January, and no new patients have been admitted since March 2024.
body: Germany's pharmacies that dispense medical cannabis want a role in the adult-use market. The Association of Cannabis-Dispensing Pharmacies (Verband der Cannabis versorgenden Apotheken, VCA) proposed on 23 November a scientifically supervised pilot in which participating pharmacies would sell cannabis to registered adults without a prescription, Newsweed and The Marijuana Herald reported.

The pitch lands in a crowded week for European cannabis policy. In France, the health minister has again pushed back the start of a permanent medical cannabis programme, telling lawmakers on 24 November that a key decree will go to the Council of State in January 2027.

Under the VCA plan, participating pharmacies would hand out prepackaged, labelled cannabis with a THC ceiling, purchase limits and age checks, only to adults who have registered for the study. Pharmacists would brief buyers on health risks. Researchers would track how consumption changes and, above all, whether a legal pharmacy channel pulls buyers away from the illicit market.

The association argues that pharmacies already have the quality-control, traceability and prevention know-how from dispensing medical cannabis. Its members say they are ready to take part once a legal basis exists, and any pilot would need government approval before a single sale. The model draws on Switzerland's pilot trials. Newsweed reported that the idea has split the profession, with some pharmacists arguing that non-medical sales clash with their public-health role.
## Streeck's comments, and what his office says

The proposal follows an 18 November interview in which Federal Drug Commissioner Hendrik Streeck (CDU), asked about pharmacy sales, pointed to Germany's roughly five million cannabis users and questioned whether they should keep buying from dealers. Several outlets read that as openness to pharmacy sales. His office has since told the pharmacy press that he has not endorsed the idea.

Streeck said in June that he could support pilot projects under tight conditions: access only from age 25, limited quantities, no advertising and scientific monitoring. But the legal route has failed before. In February 2026 the Federal Office for Agriculture and Food (BLE) rejected the 'Legalis' pharmacy-sales project in Wiesbaden, citing an insufficient legal basis.

Germany legalised possession and home growing in April 2024: adults may carry 25 grams, keep 50 grams at home and grow three plants, and non-profit cultivation clubs are allowed. Commercial adult-use sales are still banned, so the medical channel has carried much of the demand. Streeck has said medical cannabis imports are expected to exceed 300 tonnes this year. As we reported on 18 November, imports were about 201 tonnes in 2025, so 300 tonnes would be a rise of roughly 50% in a single year.

That growth is why Berlin's medical reform, which would require an in-person consultation for a first prescription and ban mail-order flower, remains stuck between the CDU and the SPD. A legal adult-use pilot is one answer to the question the reform raises: if medical channels close, where do adult consumers go?
> Germany's pharmacists are offering to become the legal shop the 2024 law never built; the question is whether Berlin wants one.
## France: another date for medical cannabis

In Paris, Renaissance deputy Nicole Dubré-Chirat asked the government on 24 November how much longer patients must wait. Health Minister Stéphanie Rist replied that the decree organising product evaluation by the Haute Autorité de Santé (HAS) will be submitted to the Council of State in January, according to Newsweed. She gave no date for when the permanent programme would actually start.

The commitment repeats what Rist told senators on 16 November, when the Senate voted for a report on the missing decrees, as we reported on 17 November. What is new is the patient count. Rist said only about 400 patients are still receiving treatment through the 2021 pilot, down from 700 in early January.

France's timeline has slipped repeatedly. The pilot opened in March 2021 and closed to new patients on 27 March 2024. The 2024 social security law promised a permanent framework from 1 January 2025 at the earliest. In January 2026, a government minister told the National Assembly that the decree on cannabis-based medicines had been cleared by the Council of State and would be published together with the reimbursement decree. Neither has appeared. Without the evaluation decree, the HAS cannot give its opinion and companies cannot start the path to market.

For EU-GMP producers, the two countries point in different directions. Germany's medical market keeps growing despite political pressure, and a pharmacy pilot, if one were ever approved, would add a new regulated channel. France, a market of 68 million people, remains closed to new medical patients almost six years after its pilot began, and the earliest realistic start for reimbursed prescriptions has moved into 2027, a presidential election year.

Watch whether any German state or city files a VCA-style pilot application, and how the BLE treats it after rejecting Wiesbaden. Watch the stalled German medical reform in the Bundestag. In France, watch for the evaluation decree reaching the Council of State in January 2027, and for the Senate-requested report, which would have to list every missing text and its timetable.
